title: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
summary: Compress embeddings to one bit per dimension: sign bits with Hamming distance and rescoring, then RaBitQ's random rotation, unbiased estimator, O(1/sqrt(D)) bound and multi-bit extension.
outcomes: Compute a binary code, its Hamming distance and the sign dot product D - 2H for a small vector pair
Explain why oversampling plus rescoring recovers recall, and why sign bits fail on non-centered data
Trace RaBitQ encoding: centering, random rotation, sign bits and the stored <o-bar,o> factor
Compute RaBitQ's unbiased estimate and explain why its error shrinks as 1/sqrt(D)
Choose between plain BQ, RaBitQ and extended RaBitQ given memory, recall and rescoring limits

lessons.title: Plain binary quantization: one sign bit per dimension

blocks.md: In product quantization you compressed vectors by splitting them into sub-vectors and storing a centroid ID per piece. This course goes to the extreme: **one bit per dimension**. The motivation is memory. One million 1024-dimensional float32 embeddings take 1,000,000 x 1024 x 4 bytes = **4.1 GB**. Stored as one bit per dimension they take **128 MB**, a 32x cut, small enough to keep in RAM and scan quickly.

scenes.caption: float32 stores 4 bytes per dimension: 4096 bytes per vector. int8 scalar quantization stores 1 byte per dimension: 1024 bytes, a 4x cut.
Binary quantization keeps 1 bit per dimension: 1024 bits = 128 bytes, exactly 32x smaller than float32.
RaBitQ (lessons 3 to 5) also stores 1 bit per dimension plus two float32 correction factors per vector: 136 bytes, about 30x smaller.

blocks.md: The simplest scheme, used by the Hugging Face sentence-transformers `quantize_embeddings` function, thresholds every coordinate at zero: the bit is 1 if the value is positive and 0 otherwise. A 1024-dimensional vector becomes a 1024-bit string, which is sixteen 64-bit words.

To compare two bit strings, count the positions where they differ. That count is the **Hamming distance**. On a CPU it is an XOR of the two words (1 wherever bits differ) followed by **popcount**, an instruction that counts the 1 bits in a word. For 1024 bits that is 16 XORs and 16 popcounts, with no floating-point math at all.

blocks.title: From floats to bits to Hamming distance (D = 8)

scenes.caption: A toy query and document with 8 dimensions. Their cosine similarity is 0.979: they point in almost the same direction.
Threshold at zero: positive values become 1, the rest 0. Each 4-byte float is now one bit.
Dimension 2 is the only disagreement: 0.05 in the query versus -0.04 in the document. Two tiny values on opposite sides of zero flip a whole bit.
XOR marks the differing positions, and popcount of the XOR gives the Hamming distance: H = 1.

blocks.md: If you map bit 1 to +1 and bit 0 to -1, the dot product of two such sign vectors is a simple function of the Hamming distance $H$: each agreeing position adds +1 and each disagreeing position adds -1.

blocks.caption: For sign vectors s and t of length D. Ranking by smallest Hamming distance is the same as ranking by largest sign dot product (Qdrant's docs use the same identity).

blocks.prompt: Three more documents have true cosine similarity to the query of 0.862 (B), 0.128 (C) and 0.905 (D). Their Hamming distances to the query are B = 2, C = 2 and D = 1, with A = 1. What does a pure Hamming ranking get wrong?
blocks.reveal: It cannot separate **B from C**: both have H = 2, even though B is a near match (0.862) and C is nearly unrelated (0.128). A and D also tie at H = 1. With 8 bits there are only 9 possible distances, so ties are common. Real embeddings have far more bits, but the same coarseness shows up among close candidates, which is exactly where ranking matters.

blocks.title: Bit agreement vs true cosine for docs A to D

scenes.caption: Fraction of matching bits, (D - H) / D. A and D tie at 0.875, B and C tie at 0.75.
True cosine similarity of the float vectors: 0.979, 0.862, 0.128, 0.905. The bits lost the gap between B and C entirely.

blocks.md: Sign bits only carry information if coordinates are spread around zero. Qdrant's docs say binary quantization needs a *centered distribution* of vector components. If every coordinate is positive, every bit is 1 and all vectors look identical; non-negative data such as SIFT image descriptors comes close to this. Lesson 2 measures this failure.
Binary quantization = sign of each coordinate, compared with XOR and popcount. It buys 32x memory and very cheap comparisons, but the distance it produces is coarse and has no error guarantee.

blocks.question: Two 1024-bit codes have Hamming distance 312. What is the dot product of the corresponding +1/-1 sign vectors?
blocks.explain: Dot = D - 2H = 1024 - 624 = 400. Each of the 712 agreeing positions adds +1 and each of the 312 differing positions adds -1: 712 - 312 = 400.

blocks.question: Which data would make plain sign-bit quantization nearly useless?
options: Unit-normalized text embeddings with coordinates spread around zero
Vectors with 4096 dimensions instead of 1024
Queries that are not in the indexed set
Vectors whose coordinates are all non-negative, such as histogram features
blocks.explain: With all coordinates at or above zero, almost every bit is 1, so codes barely differ. More dimensions helps binary quantization (more bits), and unseen queries are the normal case.

lessons.title: Binary search plus rescoring: oversample, then re-rank

blocks.md: Because Hamming distance is coarse, nobody returns binary results directly. The standard pipeline has two stages. **Stage 1** scans the compact binary codes and keeps more candidates than you need. **Stage 2** recomputes the similarity of just those candidates with more precise vectors and returns the best $k$. The extra fetch is set by **oversampling** (Qdrant, a factor), the **rescore multiplier** (sentence-transformers, a factor) or **rescoreLimit** (Weaviate, an absolute number of objects).

scenes.caption: The float query is thresholded into bits, just like the stored vectors.
Stage 1 scans every binary code (or walks an index over them) using XOR and popcount. This is the cheap part.
Keep k x oversampling candidates. In Qdrant's example, limit 100 with oversampling 2.4 pre-selects 240 vectors.
Stage 2 fetches only those candidates' original vectors and scores them against the float query. If originals live on disk, this step costs one random read per candidate.
Return the best k by exact similarity. Recall now depends on whether the true neighbors made it into the candidate set.

blocks.md: How much does stage 2 recover? The sentence-transformers team measured `mxbai-embed-large-v1` on the MTEB retrieval benchmarks: binary embeddings kept **92.53%** of float32 retrieval quality, and rescoring the top results with the float32 query against the binary document vectors raised that to **96.45%**, with memory cut 32x. Qdrant reports 0.98 recall@100 with 4x oversampling for 1536-dimensional OpenAI `text-embedding-ada-002` vectors.

To see the knob directly, I ran a small simulation (numpy, fixed seed): 20,000 synthetic vectors with D = 1024, generated from 64 latent factors plus noise, and 200 queries. Ground truth is the exact top 10 by cosine. Stage 1 ranks by Hamming distance, stage 2 rescores with exact cosine on the original vectors.

blocks.prompt: With oversampling 1 (fetch exactly 10 candidates, then rescore them), does recall@10 improve over returning the Hamming top 10 directly?
blocks.reveal: **No.** Recall@10 only asks which 10 items you returned, and rescoring 10 candidates just reorders the same 10. In the simulation both give **0.562**. Rescoring can only improve the *set* when you fetch more than k. (Hugging Face saw a gain at multiplier 1 because they rescored a top 100 and scored NDCG@10, which rewards better order and lets rescoring change which items reach the top 10.)

scenes.caption: Centered data (half the bits are 1): recall climbs from 0.562 to 0.759, 0.917 and 0.982 as stage 1 hands more candidates to stage 2. Simplified synthetic data, not a real embedding model.
Same data shifted so most coordinates are positive (88.5% of bits are 1). Hamming distance is nearly uninformative: 0.179, 0.274, 0.384, 0.52. Oversampling cannot rescue a broken first stage cheaply.

blocks.md: Two details matter in practice. First, **what you rescore with**. Qdrant and Weaviate rescore with the original float vectors, which must be stored somewhere: Qdrant warns that rescoring can significantly slow search when originals are on disk. The Hugging Face demo over 41 million Wikipedia texts keeps a 5.2 GB binary index in memory and loads int8 vectors for the top 40 from a 47.5 GB on-disk index. Second, the query does not have to be binary: scoring a float or int8 query against binary documents (**asymmetric** scoring) keeps more information at no storage cost.
Oversampling is a query-time knob: it trades speed for recall without rebuilding the index. Tune it on held-out queries for your own data, since the right value varies by model and dimension.

blocks.question: Your binary index is in RAM and original vectors are on an SSD. Recall is too low at oversampling 2. What is the main cost of raising oversampling to 8?
options: The binary index gets 4x larger
Queries must be re-embedded
Stage 2 reads about 4x more original vectors from disk per query
The Hamming scan must use floating-point math
blocks.explain: The binary scan cost barely changes. Stage 2 work, mostly random SSD reads of original vectors, grows with the number of candidates, so going from 2k to 8k candidates is about 4x more reads.

blocks.question: Why does binary quantization pair so naturally with rescoring, compared with int8 scalar quantization?
options: Binary distances are coarse with many ties, so a cheap wide first pass plus a precise second pass recovers most quality
Binary codes cannot be stored in RAM without rescoring
Rescoring is impossible with int8 vectors
Binary distances are biased upward, and rescoring subtracts the bias
blocks.explain: 1 bit per dimension loses a lot of ranking detail, so the first stage is best used as a filter. Rescoring works with int8 too (Hugging Face shows it), it just matters less there.

lessons.title: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs

blocks.md: RaBitQ (Jianyang Gao and Cheng Long, SIGMOD 2024) also stores a $D$-bit string per vector, but it designs the codebook so that the distance estimate is **unbiased** and has a **proven error bound**. The paper's motivation is that PQ and its variants have no error bound and can fail badly: on the MSong dataset, PQ's fast-scan variant had over 50% average relative error in estimated distances and could not reach 60% recall even with re-ranking.

**Step 1: normalize.** Let $c$ be a centroid (in practice the IVF cluster centroid the vector belongs to). RaBitQ quantizes the unit vector $o = (o_r - c)/\|o_r - c\|$, and likewise the query becomes $q = (q_r - c)/\|q_r - c\|$. The squared distance between raw vectors then depends only on two stored norms and one inner product of unit vectors:

blocks.caption: Equation (2) of the paper. The norm to the centroid is stored per vector; the query's norm is computed once per query. Everything reduces to estimating the unit inner product.

blocks.md: **Step 2: the codebook.** The candidate quantized vectors are the $2^D$ corners of a hypercube scaled onto the unit sphere: every coordinate is $+1/\sqrt{D}$ or $-1/\sqrt{D}$. Centering by $c$ is what fixes the all-positive failure from lesson 1, since coordinates of $o_r - c$ are spread around zero.

blocks.prompt: Without any rotation, how well does this hypercube codebook fit the vector (1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0) in D = 8? Its best corner is (1, 1, ..., 1) scaled by 1/sqrt(8). Guess the inner product between the vector and its quantized vector.
blocks.reveal: Only $1/\sqrt{8} = 0.354$, a squared distance of $2 - 2/\sqrt{8} = 1.293$. A vector like (1, 1, ..., 1)/sqrt(8) would be quantized perfectly (inner product 1). A fixed codebook favors some directions and is terrible for others, so any error bound would depend on the data.

blocks.md: **Step 3: rotate.** RaBitQ samples a random orthogonal matrix $P$ (a rotation, a form of Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform) and uses the rotated corners $P x$ as the codebook. A uniformly random rotation can send any corner anywhere on the sphere, so no direction is favored. Only $P$ is stored; the $2^D$ codewords are never materialized.

Finding the nearest rotated corner is cheap. Rotations preserve inner products, so $\langle o, P x\rangle = \langle P^{-1} o, x\rangle$: apply the inverse rotation to the data vector once, then the best corner just copies the **signs** of $o' = P^{-1} o$. The stored code is those $D$ sign bits.

blocks.title: Encoding one unit vector with RaBitQ (D = 8)

scenes.caption: A spiky unit vector: most of its length sits in dimension 0. Signs taken directly would match it with inner product only 0.673.
Apply the inverse of a random rotation (seed 11). The length is now spread across all 8 coordinates; the vector still has norm 1.
The code is the sign pattern of o': 11100110. That is the whole per-dimension payload, 1 bit each.
The bits stand for the corner x-bar with entries plus or minus 1/sqrt(8) = 0.354. Its inner product with o' is sum of |o'_i| / sqrt(8) = 0.873, far better than 0.673 without rotation.

blocks.caption: Here o-bar = P x-bar is the quantized vector. This value is computed once at index time and stored next to the code. For random rotations its expectation is about 0.798 to 0.800 for D from 100 to 1,000,000 (0.823 at D = 8).

blocks.md: Per vector, RaBitQ therefore stores the $D$-bit code plus two floats: $\|o_r - c\|$ and $\langle \bar o, o\rangle$. The paper pads the code length to the next multiple of 64 so codes fit 64-bit words. Index time is similar to PQ: on GIST (one million 960-dimensional vectors, 32 threads) the paper reports 117 s for RaBitQ, 105 s for PQ and 291 s for OPQ.

The rotation does not make every vector quantize well on every draw. It makes the quality *random with a known distribution*, the same for every input direction. That is what turns "works on my dataset" into a guarantee that holds regardless of the data.
RaBitQ indexing: center and normalize, apply one random rotation, store the sign bits plus two floats per vector. The codebook is the rotated hypercube, so no k-means training is needed.

blocks.question: Why does RaBitQ apply P^-1 to each data vector instead of rotating the codebook?
options: Rotating 2^D codewords is impossible to store or search; rotating one vector and reading its signs finds the same nearest codeword
P^-1 is cheaper to compute than P
The codebook must stay axis-aligned for popcount to work
It makes the code shorter than D bits
blocks.explain: Inner products are invariant under rotation, so maximizing over P x is the same as maximizing over x against P^-1 o, which is solved by copying signs. The codebook stays conceptual.

blocks.question: After rotation, the inner product between a data vector and its quantized vector is about 0.8 in high dimensions. What does this number mean?
options: The code is wrong in 20% of the bits
The estimator is accurate to within 0.2
The quantized vector is a unit vector at roughly 37 degrees from the data vector, so using it directly would shrink inner products
Only 80% of vectors get a valid code
blocks.explain: Both are unit vectors and their cosine is about 0.8 (about 37 degrees). Lesson 4 shows why treating o-bar as if it were o is biased, and how dividing by this stored 0.8-ish value fixes it.

lessons.title: The unbiased estimator and its O(1/sqrt(D)) error

blocks.md: At query time we want $\langle o, q\rangle$ but only have the code. The obvious move, and what PQ does, is to pretend the quantized vector is the data vector and use $\langle \bar o, q\rangle$. RaBitQ instead looks at the geometry. Split $q$ into its part along $o$ and a unit direction $e_1$ orthogonal to $o$. The paper's Lemma 3.1 gives:

blocks.tex: \langle \bar o, q\rangle = \langle \bar o, o\rangle\,\langle o, q\rangle + \langle \bar o, e_1\rangle\,\sqrt{1 - \langle o, q\rangle^2}
blocks.caption: Exact for any three unit vectors. The first term is the signal, scaled by about 0.8. The second term is noise: its factor is the projection of the random o-bar onto a direction orthogonal to o.

blocks.md: Dividing by the stored $\langle \bar o, o\rangle$ removes the scaling. Because the rotation is uniformly random, $\langle \bar o, e_1\rangle$ is symmetric around 0, so the leftover error term has expectation exactly 0. That gives the RaBitQ estimator:

blocks.tex: \widehat{\langle o, q\rangle} = \frac{\langle \bar o, q\rangle}{\langle \bar o, o\rangle} = \langle o, q\rangle + \sqrt{1 - \langle o, q\rangle^2}\;\frac{\langle \bar o, e_1\rangle}{\langle \bar o, o\rangle}
blocks.caption: Theorem 3.2: E[estimate] equals the true inner product. Through equation (2) this also gives an unbiased estimate of squared Euclidean distance.

blocks.md: Back to the toy from lesson 3 (seed 11). The query, after the same inverse rotation and normalization, has true inner product $\langle o, q\rangle = 0.688$ with the data vector. The code gives $\langle \bar o, q\rangle = 0.530$ and the stored factor is $\langle \bar o, o\rangle = 0.873$, so the estimate is $0.530 / 0.873 = 0.607$, an error of -0.080. A different rotation (seed 32) gives $0.395 / 0.886 = 0.446$, error -0.242. At D = 8 single estimates are noisy. The claim is about the average and about how the noise shrinks with D.

blocks.title: Toy pair, D = 8, averaged over 20,000 random rotations

scenes.caption: The target: the true inner product of the toy pair is 0.688.
Treating the quantized vector as the data vector averages 0.567: biased low by the factor E<o-bar,o>, which is 0.823 at D = 8.
Dividing by the stored <o-bar,o> averages 0.688, matching the truth. Individual draws still scatter (standard deviation 0.195 at D = 8).

blocks.md: How big is the noise? The paper shows that $\langle \bar o, e_1\rangle$ concentrates within $O(1/\sqrt{D})$ of 0. With probability at least $1 - 2e^{-c_0 \epsilon_0^2}$ the error obeys:

blocks.tex: \left|\frac{\langle \bar o, q\rangle}{\langle \bar o, o\rangle} - \langle o, q\rangle\right| \le \sqrt{\frac{1 - \langle \bar o, o\rangle^2}{\langle \bar o, o\rangle^2}}\cdot\frac{\epsilon_0}{\sqrt{D-1}} = O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}\right)
blocks.caption: Equations (14) to (16). The paper fixes epsilon_0 = 1.9 for all datasets. Alon and Klartag (FOCS 2017) showed no D-bit code can beat O(1/sqrt(D)), so the bound is asymptotically optimal.

scenes.caption: Dots: measured standard deviation of the error over 4,000 random rotations per D, true inner product 0.688. The curve sqrt(1 - ip^2) x 0.755 / sqrt(D - 1) is a first-order approximation using E<o-bar,o> = 0.798.
Each 4x increase in D halves the error: 0.140 at D = 16, 0.0689 at 64, 0.0338 at 256, 0.0171 at 1024. Higher-dimensional embeddings are easier for 1-bit codes.
Pairs that are nearly orthogonal (ip near 0) have the largest error; near-duplicates (ip near 1) have almost none, because the noise term is scaled by sqrt(1 - ip^2).
The bound with eps0 = 1.9 and <o-bar,o> = 0.8 sits at about 1.9 standard deviations, 1.9x the typical error at ip = 0,, and it is what RaBitQ uses to decide re-ranking (lesson 5).

blocks.md: The paper picked $\epsilon_0 = 1.9$ because, in its experiments, deciding re-ranking with this bound gave nearly perfect recall of the true nearest neighbor. That is not the same as covering every pair: in my simulation the 1.9 interval missed the true value for about 1% of pairs at $\langle o, q\rangle = 0.69$ and about 6% at $\langle o, q\rangle = 0$. Near neighbors are the pairs that matter for search, and their larger inner products give smaller errors.

Unbiased does not mean accurate on each pair. It means the errors average out to zero instead of pushing every estimate the same way. Per-pair accuracy comes from concentration: the 1/sqrt(D) shrinkage.

blocks.question: RaBitQ errors at D = 256 are too large for you. Following the 1/sqrt(D) rule, how many code bits per vector would halve the error?
blocks.explain: Error scales as 1/sqrt(D), so halving it needs 4x the bits: 1024. The paper notes you can lengthen codes by padding vectors with zeros before rotation; padded dimensions are not kept in the raw vectors.

blocks.question: A colleague estimates inner products with <o-bar,q> directly, skipping the division. What happens to a ranking of documents for one query?
options: Nothing; the ranking is identical because every estimate is scaled by exactly the same constant
Estimates become unbiased but noisier
Each document's estimate is scaled by its own <o-bar,o>, which varies per vector, so the ranking gets extra noise and the distances are biased
The code must be recomputed
blocks.explain: The scaling factor is not a global constant: it is about 0.8 on average but differs from vector to vector, because it depends on how evenly each rotated vector spreads its length. The paper also notes this direct estimator is provably biased, which matters when plugged into equation (2) for distances.

lessons.title: Computing the estimate with popcount, and re-ranking by the bound

blocks.md: The estimator needs $\langle \bar o, q\rangle = \langle \bar x, q'\rangle$ where $q' = P^{-1} q$ is computed once per query. Since the estimate is approximate anyway, RaBitQ also quantizes $q'$: with $v_l = \min_i q'_i$, $v_r = \max_i q'_i$ and step $\Delta = (v_r - v_l)/(2^{B_q} - 1)$, each coordinate becomes a $B_q$-bit integer $\bar q_u[i]$. The paper uses **randomized rounding** (round up with probability equal to the fractional part) so the query quantization stays unbiased, and proves $B_q = \Theta(\log\log D)$ bits suffice. In practice $B_q = 4$; Faiss uses `qb = 4` by default.

For the toy query, $v_l = -0.403$, $v_r = 0.514$, $\Delta = 0.0612$, and rounding gives $\bar q_u$ = (6, 6, 15, 8, 10, 15, 15, 0). (For a readable toy I rounded to nearest; RaBitQ rounds randomly.) Expanding the inner product of a sign vector with an affine-quantized vector gives terms that are all precomputed except one integer dot product:

blocks.tex: \langle \bar x, \bar q\rangle = \frac{2\Delta}{\sqrt D}\langle \bar x_b, \bar q_u\rangle + \frac{2 v_l}{\sqrt D}\sum_i \bar x_b[i] - \frac{\Delta}{\sqrt D}\sum_i \bar q_u[i] - \sqrt D\, v_l
blocks.caption: Equation (20). The popcount of the code is stored at index time; the sum of the query integers is computed once per query. Only the dot product of bits with small integers is per vector.

blocks.md: Split each 4-bit query integer into 4 bit planes. Then $\langle \bar x_b, \bar q_u\rangle = \sum_j 2^j\,\mathrm{popcount}(\bar x_b \,\&\, \text{plane}_j)$: four AND plus popcount passes over $D$-bit strings, the same instructions plain binary quantization uses.

blocks.title: Bit-plane dot product for the toy (D = 8, Bq = 4)
blocks.code:
xb = [1,1,1,0,0,1,1,0]          # data code: signs of o'
qu = [6,6,15,8,10,15,15,0]       # query, 4-bit integers
acc = 0
for j in range(4):               # one pass per bit plane
    plane = [(v >> j) & 1 for v in qu]
    both = [a & b for a, b in zip(xb, plane)]
    acc += (1 << j) * sum(both)  # sum(both) = popcount
# acc == dot(xb, qu) == 57

scenes.caption: The data code from lesson 3 and the 4-bit query. In real code each list is packed into 64-bit words.
Plane 0 holds the lowest bit of each query integer. AND with the code keeps positions where both are 1: popcount 3, weight 1.
Plane 1: popcount 5, weight 2, so acc grows by 10.
Plane 2: popcount 5, weight 4, adds 20.
Plane 3: popcount 3, weight 8, adds 24. Total 57, equal to the direct dot product 6+6+15+15+15 of the query values where the code is 1.

blocks.md: Plugging in (code popcount 5, query sum 75) gives $\langle \bar x, \bar q\rangle = 0.558$ versus 0.530 with the float query, so the estimate is $0.558/0.873 = 0.640$ instead of 0.607. At D = 8 with nearest rounding, query quantization error is visible; averaged over 20,000 randomized roundings the value is 0.530, unbiased. For a single code, the paper reports this bitwise path is on average about 3x faster than PQ and OPQ looking up tables in RAM at the same accuracy. For packed batches of 32 codes, RaBitQ reuses PQ's SIMD **FastScan** layout by treating each 4 bits of the code as a sub-segment with a 16-entry lookup table.

**Re-ranking by the bound.** PQ systems re-rank a fixed number of candidates, a knob that must be tuned per dataset. RaBitQ turns its error bound into a lower bound on each candidate's distance. Scanning candidates, it computes the exact distance only if that lower bound is below the best exact distance found so far; otherwise the candidate is provably (with high probability) not the nearest neighbor and is dropped.

blocks.title: Bound-based re-ranking for one query (simulated, D = 1024, K = 1)

scenes.caption: The 8 candidates with the smallest estimated squared distance, from the synthetic dataset of lesson 2 (unit vectors, one global centroid, eps0 = 1.9). Each lower bound is the estimated distance minus its error bound.
No exact distance is known yet, so the first candidate is re-ranked: exact 1.100. Best so far = 1.100.
Candidates 2 to 5 have lower bounds 1.019 to 1.099, all below 1.100, so each might still be closer. Re-rank them: none beats 1.100.
Candidates 6 to 8 have lower bounds 1.109, 1.132 and 1.141, above the best exact 1.100. They are dropped without touching their raw vectors.

Over all 20,000 vectors, only 5 exact distances were computed and the true nearest neighbor (exact 1.100) was found. Simplified: the paper does this inside probed IVF clusters with per-cluster centroids.

blocks.md: Per vector, the query-time work is a few AND plus popcount passes over the D-bit code and a handful of multiply-adds with precomputed factors. The error bound then tells you which candidates are worth an exact distance.

blocks.question: Why can the error bound replace the usual 'rerank the top R candidates' hyperparameter?
options: The bound gives each candidate a lower bound on its distance, so you can skip exactly those that cannot beat the best exact distance found so far
The bound makes every estimate exact
The bound tells you the optimal R for each dataset ahead of time
Re-ranking is not needed for RaBitQ at all
blocks.explain: A fixed R must be tuned and can be too small on hard data (the paper shows no single R works across datasets). The bound adapts per query: easy queries re-rank few vectors, hard ones more.

blocks.question: RaBitQ quantizes the query to 4-bit integers. What does it gain, and why is it safe?
options: It shrinks the index 4x; safe because queries are not stored
It makes the estimator exact; safe because rounding is random
It removes the need for the rotation
It turns the per-vector float dot product into a few AND plus popcount passes; safe because the added error is much smaller than the estimator's own O(1/sqrt(D)) error
blocks.explain: The code is already a 1-bit approximation, so computing its inner product in full float precision is overkill. Theorem 3.3 shows Theta(log log D) query bits keep the added error at the same order, and 4 bits made it negligible in the paper's tests.

lessons.title: Extended RaBitQ, and binary quantization in real systems

blocks.md: How much of RaBitQ's advantage comes from the rotation and centering? Back to the lesson 2 simulation, now comparing three first stages at the same 1 bit per dimension, each followed by exact rescoring: plain Hamming (binary query), plain sign codes scored against the float query (asymmetric), and RaBitQ (global centroid, one random rotation, float query, estimator).

blocks.title: Simulated recall@10, 1 bit per dimension, D = 1024

scenes.caption: Oversampling 1. On centered data, an asymmetric float query lifts sign codes from 0.562 to 0.708, and RaBitQ matches it (0.708). On shifted data, sign codes collapse (0.179, 0.292) while RaBitQ holds at 0.718.
Oversampling 2: 0.759, 0.911, 0.912 centered; 0.274, 0.428, 0.929 shifted.

Oversampling 4: 0.917, 0.987, 0.987 centered; 0.384, 0.586, 0.991 shifted. Simplified synthetic data: on well-behaved embeddings plain asymmetric binary is already strong; RaBitQ's edge is robustness.

blocks.md: **Extended RaBitQ** (Gao, Gou, Xu, Yang, Long and Wong, arXiv 2409.09913) answers the obvious next question: what if 32x is too aggressive and you want high recall *without* keeping raw vectors for re-ranking? It uses $B$ bits per dimension. The codebook is a uniform grid of $B$-bit unsigned integers, shifted to be symmetric around 0, normalized onto the unit sphere and randomly rotated. Because codewords are still randomly rotated unit vectors, the same estimator and its unbiasedness carry over.

Encoding is harder than copying signs: the method searches over a rescaling factor $t$ for the grid point whose direction best matches $o'$, in $O(2^B \cdot D \log D)$ time. A neat property: the most significant bit of each $B$-bit code is exactly the sign bit, so the 1-bit RaBitQ code is embedded inside every extended code.

blocks.title: A 3-bit extended code for the toy vector (D = 8)

scenes.caption: The same rotated vector as lesson 3, and its 1-bit RaBitQ code 11100110 with <o-bar,o> = 0.873.
With B = 3, each coordinate maps to an integer 0 to 7 (grid values -3.5 to 3.5, shifted by 3.5). A search over the scale t finds 5,6,7,3,3,4,7,0, with <o-bar,o> = 0.995.
Values 4 to 7 are the positive grid points, so the top bit is the sign: 11100110, identical to the 1-bit code. The toy estimate improves from 0.607 to 0.719 (true 0.688).

blocks.md: The paper stores the top bits separately. At query time it first estimates every candidate from the top bits alone with the fast 1-bit path, drops candidates the bound rules out, and reads the remaining bits only for survivors. It proves the bits needed are asymptotically optimal and gives an empirical formula: with over 99.9% probability the inner-product error is below $2^{-B} \cdot 5.75/\sqrt{D}$. In its experiments $B = 5$ (about 6.4x compression) stably gave over 95% recall and $B = 7$ (about 4.5x) over 99%, without re-ranking on raw vectors.

blocks.title: Extended RaBitQ empirical error bound vs bits per dimension

scenes.caption: At D = 1024 the bound is 0.090 for B = 1 and halves with every extra bit: 0.0056 at B = 5 and 0.0014 at B = 7. The formula is fitted from the paper's experiments, not a theorem.
At D = 128 every value is sqrt(8) = 2.83x larger: low-dimensional vectors need more bits per dimension for the same accuracy.
At D = 3072 the curve drops by another 1.73x relative to 1024. Each extra bit buys a 2x reduction, while 1/sqrt(D) gains come only from more dimensions.

blocks.md:
**In real systems** (as their docs describe today):

- **Faiss** has `IndexRaBitQ` and `IndexIVFRaBitQ`, with an `nb_bits` option for multi-bit codes and a query-bits setting `qb` that defaults to 4. The index factory accepts strings such as `IVF4096,RaBitQ` or `RaBitQ4`, and a `RaBitQfs` FastScan variant.
- **Weaviate** offers rotational quantization (RQ) at 8, 4 and 1 bits. Its docs say RQ is inspired by extended RaBitQ but uses fast pseudorandom rotations; 1-bit RQ stores data signs and quantizes queries to 5 bits, and works on datasets like SIFT where BQ performs poorly. It also has plain BQ and over-fetches then rescores.
- **Qdrant** offers binary quantization at 1, 1.5 and 2 bits per dimension, asymmetric scoring with a scalar-quantized query, and `oversampling` plus `rescore` search parameters.

Choosing: plain BQ is simplest and fastest when embeddings are high-dimensional and centered, and you can afford rescoring. RaBitQ-style rotation plus correction factors costs a few bytes per vector and makes 1-bit codes robust on skewed data. Multi-bit (extended RaBitQ, 4-bit RQ) is the route when you want to drop raw vectors from RAM entirely.

blocks.question: You must serve 1536-dimensional embeddings with over 95% recall and cannot keep float vectors anywhere (no RAM, no disk) for rescoring. Which option fits best?
options: 1-bit binary quantization with oversampling 8
Plain BQ with a Hamming-only ranking
1-bit RaBitQ with error-bound re-ranking
Extended RaBitQ with about 5 bits per dimension
blocks.explain: Every 1-bit option relies on re-ranking with stored originals to reach high recall. Extended RaBitQ was designed for this case: the paper reports B = 5 stably gives over 95% recall without raw-vector re-ranking.

blocks.question: An extended RaBitQ index stores 7-bit codes. Why does storing the most significant bits in a separate array speed up search?
options: The top bits form the 1-bit RaBitQ code, so a fast 1-bit estimate plus its bound can prune most candidates before the remaining 6 bits are read
It lets the index skip the random rotation
The most significant bits never change between queries
It halves the storage
blocks.explain: The top bit of each dimension equals the sign code. A cheap first pass on those bits, with the error bound, discards candidates that cannot qualify, and only survivors pay for the full-precision estimate.
